```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(ggbeeswarm)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
person <- read_csv(file.path(res, "scores_per_person.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
models <- read_csv(file.path(res, "model_comparison.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, c("microbiome only", "host only", "both")))
rocs <- read_csv(file.path(res, "roc_curves.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, c("microbiome only", "host only", "both")))
auc_of <- function(m) sprintf("%.2f", models$auc[models$model == m])
mcol <- c(`microbiome only` = pal[["teal"]], `host only` = pal[["orange"]], both = pal[["navy"]])
ocol <- c(preterm = pal[["orange"]], term = pal[["navy"]])
```

## So far, one table at a time {.center}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4
week <- tribble(
  ~day, ~what,
  "Tue AM", "shape, depth, filtering",
  "Tue PM", "differential testing",
  "Wed PM", "distances and ordination",
  "Thu PM", "sets and enrichment"
) |>
  mutate(x = row_number())
week |>
  cross_join(tibble(tbl = c("species table", "gene table"), y = c(2, 1))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = tbl), width = 0.92, height = 0.85, colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = tbl), colour = "white", size = 8) +
  geom_text(data = week, aes(x, 2.95, label = paste0(day, "\n", what)),
            size = 6.5, lineheight = 0.95, colour = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`species table` = pal[["teal"]], `gene table` = pal[["orange"]]),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 3.5)) +
  theme_void()
```

We ran every method this week twice, once on each table, and never on both
together.

## Today's question {.center}

Does putting the two tables together tell you anything that neither told you
alone?

. . .

Sometimes, and you can measure when.

## When combining helps

::: {.incremental}
- If both tables carry the **same** information, combining them adds nothing
  beyond a slightly better estimate of that one thing.
- If they carry **different** information, combining them can add a lot.
- If one carries **nothing**, combining them makes your model worse, because you
  spent degrees of freedom on noise.
:::

. . .

So before fitting any model, measure how much the two tables already agree.

## One number per person, from each table

```{r}
#| eval: false
# from the species table: how anaerobic is this person, on average
micro_score <- per_sample |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(micro = mean(1 - lacto_fraction))

# from the gene table: how inflamed, using Thursday's gene set
host_score <- per_sample |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(host = mean(inflammatory_score))
```

The two tables have 14,446 rows between them. After this step they are two
columns, one row per person:

```{r}
#| echo: false
person |>
  select(participant_id, outcome, micro_score, host_score) |>
  head(3) |>
  mutate(across(c(micro_score, host_score), ~ sprintf("%.2f", .x))) |>
  kable(align = "llrr")
```

## The two scores barely agree

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(person, aes(micro_score, host_score)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = outcome), size = 2.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey40", linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ocol) +
  labs(x = "mean anaerobe fraction, from the species table",
       y = "mean inflammatory score,\nfrom the gene table", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Correlation: **`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(person$micro_score, person$host_score))`**.

## Low agreement is good news here {.center}

The two tables are telling us about **different** things.

. . .

In this cohort a disturbed bacterial community and an inflamed epithelium are
separate measurements, and knowing one tells you almost nothing about the other.

. . .

So each has something to add.

## One model per table, and one with both

```{r}
#| eval: false
glm(preterm ~ micro_z,           data = per_person, family = binomial)
glm(preterm ~ host_z,            data = per_person, family = binomial)
glm(preterm ~ micro_z + host_z,  data = per_person, family = binomial)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
models |>
  transmute(model,
            AUC = sprintf("%.2f", auc),
            `95% interval` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", auc_lo, auc_hi),
            AIC = round(aic)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

- [Gene table alone: AUC `r auc_of("host only")`]{style="color: #e76f51; font-weight: 600;"}

::: {.fragment}
Adding the host score to the microbiome model:
p = `r format(models$lrt_p_vs_micro[models$model == "both"], digits = 2)`.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Two summary scores in one logistic regression are the simplest version of the
case for multiomics.
:::
:::
::::

## Significance and prediction are different questions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
On Tuesday, preterm versus term gave **1,698 significant genes**.

::: {.fragment}
Today, those same genes predict the outcome with an AUC of
`r auc_of("host only")`.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Significance asks whether the groups differ on average.
- AUC asks whether you can tell which person is in which group.
- Many small differences can give you the first without the second.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(person, aes(outcome, host_z, colour = outcome)) +
  geom_quasirandom(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.8, width = 0.3) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5, colour = "grey20",
               linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ocol, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "host score (z), per person") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 22)
```
:::
::::

## Choose the method from the goal

| if you want to | you need |
|---|---|
| improve a prediction | a model with features from both tables |
| find features that move together | correlation across tables |
| find shared sample structure | a joint ordination |
| describe a mechanism | something more than either |

: {tbl-colwidths="[45,55]"}

## Integration methods, simplest first

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
| | examples | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| simple | scores in one model | Reduce each table to a few numbers and fit one model, as we did today. Every other method has to beat this. |
| intermediate | canonical correlation, PLS, sparse PLS | Find the combination of features in table A that best tracks a combination in table B. |
| multi-block | DIABLO, MOFA | Decompose several tables at once into shared and table-specific factors. |
| similarity-based | Procrustes, co-inertia, DiSTATIS | Compare the sample configurations rather than the features. |
| networks | | Build a graph across data types and look at its structure. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,26,56]"}
:::

## The cost of each method

| | gives you | costs you |
|---|---|---|
| scores in one model | interpretability | you chose the scores by hand |
| sparse PLS | feature pairs | tuning, and unstable selection |
| DIABLO, MOFA | shared factors | sample size, and hard-to-explain factors |
| Procrustes | one agreement statistic | no features, no prediction |
| networks | a picture | almost unlimited freedom to fool yourself |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,32,44]"}

## All of them can overfit {.center}

With 157 people and 14,446 features, you can find a combination that separates
your groups perfectly.

. . .

It will not replicate.

. . .

Every method on that list needs cross-validation or a held-out set, and the
fancier the method the more it needs it.

## Our own result, honestly stated

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- We chose both scores **after** looking at the data all week.
- We never held out a test set.
- AUC `r auc_of("both")` with a 95% interval of
  `r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", models$auc_lo[models$model == "both"], models$auc_hi[models$model == "both"])`.
- The two intervals for the single-table models overlap each other.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(models, aes(auc, fct_rev(model), colour = model)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = auc_lo, xmax = auc_hi), height = 0.25, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = mcol, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "AUC with 95% interval", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 22)
```
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
The improvement is real, but we should be modest about how big it is, and say
both when we report it.
:::
